text.p: These are the leading stories in the Serbian and Montenegrin press on Friday. Reuters has not verified them nor does it vouch for their accuracy.
- SERBIA -
NASA BORBA

- Reduction of humanitarian aid to Yugoslavia from $46 million last year to $40 million in 1997 is not a major cut since the crisis is past its peak, says U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata at the end of her tour of former Yugoslav countries.
- Croatian Democratic Union supporters prevent Serbs from visiting Drvar in Bosnia, says IPTF spokesman Alun Roberts.
- Unjust solution for Kosovo could lead to another Bosnia, says Adem Demaci's Parliamentary Party of Kosova.

- Tax on apartments bought cheaply during hyperinflation in 1993, state and central bank property among possible sources of funds to repay old hard currency savings frozen since 1991, suggests Beogradska Banka Group President Borka Vucic.

- Share tax makes no sense, says Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce banking committee. Shareholders returning shares in banks because they are forced to pay tax on shares which do not bring them any dividend.
- Merrill Lynch of London discussing with Beogradska and Vojvodjanska banka issue of securities for frozen hard currency savings. Discount of 30 to 40 percent acceptable.

- Second working version of draft law on ownership transformation by the end of next week. Agricultural complex not included in the law. Differing views on rights of unemployed in the privatisation process.
- State radio and television most popular media in Serbia, opposition Studio B TV, B92 radio, Blic and Weekly Telegraf lead in Belgrade, according to a Partner marketing agency poll.
POLITIKA
- Large turnout of Serbs for elections in Eastern Slavonia, Croatia. Serbs vote to stay, says Yugoslav government.
- Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and U.N. High Commissioner for refugees Sadako Ogata agree conditions must be created for the return of refugees in former Yugoslavia to their homes.

- Yugoslavia and Slovak Republic agree advancing cooperation is in mutual interest, trade could reach around $400 million per year in both directions, says Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic on return from visit to Slovakia.
- Programmes, decisions on issue and sale of shares to be made by managements of public enterprises based on capital evaluation, but with the consent of the state as the founder.
- Will the state stand behind the collapsed Dafiment bank pyramid scheme, as its depositors are demanding?
- Cold weather, snow in central parts of Serbia threatens sown crops, orchards.
- Less free services in health sector from April 19, according to Serbian government decision.
- Labour Day to be celebrated on May 1 and 2 in Yugoslavia, under the old law on public holidays.
- Yugoslav army deputy chief of staff General Dragoljub Ojdanic and UNPREDEP commander in Macedonia Brigadier-General Bo Vranker of Sweden meet in Bujanovac, discuss cooperation.
- Agriculture is a priority in Seriba's economic development, says Serbian Agriculture Minister Jovan Babovic.
- Serbian commercial courts rule on 4,871 liquidations of firms in 1996, fines and disciplinary measures for around 5,000 managers, mainly for accounting and bookkeeping violations.
- MONTENEGRO -
POBJEDA
- Montenegrin pensioners to receive 60 percent of February pensions on Friday.
- Most schools in Montenegro on strike while hospitals and health centres hold one-hour warning strikes over unpaid winter bonus and commuting costs.
- Labour and education ministers, Branimir Bojanic and Dragan Kujovic, say the government is not in a position to pay bonuses due to budget problems.
- General strike in Radoje Dakic machine building factory from Podgorica might stop Monday, says trade union leader Rajko Vukovic after workers start receiving late salaries.
- Montenegrin commercial banks report positive 1996 results, with seven leading banks registering 7.5 million dinars of profit.
- Losses of Montenegrin economy (3,663 companies) in 1995 stood at 584.9 million dinars.
MONITOR

- President Momir Bulatovic has lost his status of colonial governor of Montenegro and become a postman between Serbian President Milosevic and Montenegrin Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic, says Montenegrin parliament speaker Svetozar Marovic, commenting on dispute in the republic's leaderhsip.
- New coastal water pipeline to be built with Slovak capital could endanger ecological balance of lake Skadar, the main source of drinking water.

- According to the constitution and statute of the ruling Democratic Party of Socialists, the Montenegrin prime minister does not have to obey the republican president's directives. -- Belgrade newsroom + 381 11 222 4305
